case_studies.title: Unprompted coordination through shared memory in LLM agents: a locked two-implementation replication and extension
case_studies.abstract: Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. Existing research tells the agents that partners exist or asks them to coordinate. Whether coordination arises through shared state alone, with nothing disclosing that anyone else is present, is the key question for deployments that share caches and memory between agents, yet it has rarely been examined, and never with independent replication; this study does both. Four agents each received a short arithmetic task and a key-value store presented to each as its own scratch space; two held complementary halves of one computation, and no prompt mentioned other agents, sharing or collaboration. For reliability, the environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis. The results bear novelty value in three respects. Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Whether a model coordinated depended not on its vendor tier but on whether it wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again, and one ordinary sentence, "check your workspace again before submitting", switched that second look on and off. The findings held under replication. For practice, state shared between agents is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged. For research, designs should be locked before the data, and the parse rule, endpoint and parameters reported. Future work should test open-weight models and separate using another agent's output from intending to communicate.
case_studies.summary: The study shows that large language‑model agents can coordinate automatically just by sharing a key‑value store, even without any explicit prompts about teamwork. They built two independent implementations of a shared memory system and proved that joint success depended on agents reading from and writing to the store. For IT infrastructure managers, this means shared caches or memory spaces can unintentionally become channels for agent communication.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If your organisation runs multiple LLM agents on shared infrastructure, isolate the agent namespaces: give each agent a dedicated key‑value store or use distinct prefixes, log all store access, and audit the data paths to prevent accidental coordination.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper investigates agent coordination via shared memory, a niche research topic with limited direct applicability to current IT engineering workflows. It offers insights but no ready-to-deploy system or clear commercial use case within 90 days.
